Work

Remote work: benefits and pitfalls

It saves commuting and gives flexibility, but can isolate you and blur work-life boundaries. Hybrid models fare well.

Since 2020, millions of people have worked from home for at least part of the week. For some it was a relief; for others, a source of loneliness and endless working days.

What the studies say

In 2024, Nicholas Bloom and colleagues published in Nature an experiment with more than 1,600 employees of a large Chinese company. Half of them, chosen at random, were allowed to work from home two days a week. After six months, their performance and promotions were the same as the rest, but they quit a third less often and were more satisfied.

Fully remote work has more lights and shadows. It saves commuting and allows uninterrupted concentration, but it can increase isolation, make informal learning from colleagues harder, especially for newcomers, and blur the line between the working day and personal life.

What usually helps

  • Create a workspace that is separate, however small, and tidy it away when you finish.
  • Set start and finish times, and take breaks.
  • Simulate the "commute": a short walk before and after work helps you switch modes.
  • Keep in touch: brief calls, cameras on at times, in-person days with the team.
  • Move: working from home greatly reduces daily physical activity.

References

  1. Bloom, N., Han, R. y Liang, J. (2024). Hybrid working from home improves retention without damaging performance. Nature, 630, 920–925.
  2. Wang, B. et al. (2021). Achieving effective remote working during the COVID-19 pandemic. Applied Psychology, 70(1), 16–59.
